analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil, gas, and mineral leasing in the Arctic Ocean.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee on December 20, 2022, with 13 days left in the Congress, and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred the Interior Department from issuing or extending any lease or authorization to explore for or produce oil, natural gas, or other minerals in Arctic areas of the federal offshore waters. It also declared it U.S. policy to keep Arctic fossil fuels in the ground to limit climate change. The bill was introduced in the final two weeks of the congressional session and died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be coastal and Indigenous Arctic communities that depend on intact marine ecosystems for subsistence hunting and fishing, the fishing and tourism economies that rely on those waters, and everyone exposed to climate change impacts, since the bill aimed to keep Arctic carbon reserves from being developed. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing or extending any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or other minerals in Arctic areas of the Outer Continental Shelf.
Declares U.S. policy that the Arctic Ocean be managed for the best interests of the American people, including keeping fossil fuels in the ground to avoid the dangerous impacts of climate change.

Cites findings that the Arctic is warming at twice the global rate and that developing Arctic Ocean oil and gas is incompatible with staying within the global carbon budget needed to avoid the worst climate effects.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on oil and gas companies that would be permanently shut out of Arctic offshore leases, on the oilfield services sector that supports offshore exploration, and on the federal treasury in the form of forgone leasing revenue. Energy consumers could face marginally higher costs if domestic offshore supply is reduced, though Arctic production has never been a large share of U.S. output.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and federal revenue

drawbacks.text: Permanently locking up federal offshore acreage reduces domestic energy supply and leasing revenue, a cost opponents of offshore restrictions routinely cite, particularly during periods of high energy prices.
The prohibition applies not just to oil and gas but to exploration or production of any mineral in Arctic federal waters, written as a broad standing prohibition rather than a time-limited pause.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: it trades potential future Arctic oil and gas production and federal leasing revenue for protecting a fragile marine ecosystem and keeping a large carbon reserve undeveloped. The climate and ecosystem case is well documented in the bill's own findings, and Arctic offshore drilling has been controversial for spill risk, so the main honest objection is the foregone energy supply — a cost that falls mostly on a single industry rather than broadly on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with two weeks left in the session and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on December 20, 2022, joined by six cosponsors (five Democrats and one independent).
The same day it was introduced, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry is better off, because Arctic federal waters remain legally open to future leasing. Nothing about the status quo changed; communities hoping to shield the Arctic from drilling gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit oil, gas, and mineral leasing in Arctic federal offshore waters.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats and independents (Warren, Wyden, Blumenthal, Sanders, Menendez, Markey)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — five Senate Democrats and the Senate's one independent.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended 13 days later.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and with no hearing or vote ever held, no recorded opposition positions exist in this record.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar them from Arctic federal offshore leases, closing a frontier area to exploration and production. Their gain from the bill's death — Arctic waters staying open to leasing — is the public's cost in spill risk and additional carbon development. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Oilfield services and offshore drilling contractors
industries.note: Exploration bans remove the contract pipeline that supports offshore rigs and services; an Arctic ban shrinks their future market. Their interest in continued leasing runs against communities bearing the spill and climate risk.
The bill's findings identify fisheries, marine mammals, and subsistence hunters as depending on intact Arctic Ocean ecosystems that an oil spill or industrial development would threaten. [S3]
